entities.name: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (c. 519 BCE – c. 430 BCE) stands as the quintessential embodiment of Roman civic virtue, a figure whose legendary selflessness and devotion to the Republic profoundly shaped the Roman identity and subsequent Western political thought. Born into a patrician family, Cincinnatus gained historical prominence in the mid-5th century BCE as a farmer who twice abandoned his plow to serve Rome as dictator during dire national emergencies, only to relinquish absolute power immediately upon resolving the crises, returning to his humble agricultural life.

His first and most celebrated dictatorship occurred in 458 BCE when the Aequi, a rival Italic tribe, besieged a Roman consular army under Minucius Esquilinus on Mount Algidus. The Roman Senate urgently summoned Cincinnatus, then toiling on his modest farm, to assume dictatorial powers. Within sixteen days, Cincinnatus assembled a new army, marched to Mount Algidus, encircled the Aequi, and forced their surrender, rescuing the trapped Roman forces. He then famously resigned his dictatorship, which was constitutionally valid for six months, after just fifteen days, demonstrating an unparalleled commitment to republican principles over personal ambition. His second, less documented dictatorship in 439 BCE saw him suppress the alleged tyrannical aspirations of Spurius Maelius, a wealthy plebeian accused of seeking to usurp power through popular support.
